blind_judge.simulator_quality: Both are plausible short, early-stage exchanges. B feels more responsive to the customer’s stated concern; neither transcript shows whether the promised follow-up actually happens.
blind_judge.summary: B is stronger because it asks what matters to the family (turn 1) and adapts when the customer says layout is the main concern (turn 2). It gives a relevant layout concept—queen-size beds are shown in all three bedrooms—and avoids guessing at exact measurements. However, the supplied facts include approximate areas for the master bedroom and two other bedrooms, so B could have shared those figures while making clear they are approximate, then offered to confirm the approved plan and furniture fit. A gives basic unit facts at turn 1, but its turn-2 response offers no useful information beyond saying the request is registered for verification; it could have shared the same approximate room areas and clearly explained what exact information it would confirm. B’s turn 3 ends naturally with the customer willing to wait, though a clear follow-up expectation would improve progression. No material factual error is evident in either transcript.
